summary: The cryptographic algorithm and key size requirements set when DKIM was designed a decade earlier had become obsolete. This document updates the requirements to what is minimally suitable for use with currently specified algorithms.

plainLanguage.summary: DKIM signs email so a recipient can check a message's signature using a key found in DNS. This RFC requires rsa-sha256, forbids rsa-sha1, and sets minimum RSA key requirements.

questions: what rsa key size should dkim use
what rsa key size does dkim require
what algorithm must dkim signers use
subtitle: DKIM requires rsa-sha256 and retires rsa-sha1 for signing and verification.

tldr.problem: DKIM's earlier algorithm and key-size requirements had become unsuitable, and SHA-1 was recognized as weak.
tldr.mechanism: Signers MUST use rsa-sha256 and RSA keys of at least 1024 bits; 2048 bits or more is recommended. Verifiers must reject keys below 1024 bits and support keys from 1024 through 4096 bits.
tldr.outcome: This Proposed Standard updates RFC 6376 and marks sha1 historic in the DKIM Hash Algorithms registry.

today: RFC 8301 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6376. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DKIM Rules Changed
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) signs hashes of email headers and content. A recipient retrieves the signature verification key from a DNS TXT record.

RFC 6376 specified RSA and recommended keys from 1024 to 2048 bits, while still requiring verification of 512-bit keys. This RFC says shorter keys weaken DKIM and that DNS software's 256-octet TXT string limit constrained larger RSA keys.
sections.plainLanguage: DKIM lets a recipient check a signature using a key published in DNS. The earlier rules still accepted keys the RFC now says are too short.

sections.title: Signing and Verification Algorithms
sections.content:
This specification defines rsa-sha1 and rsa-sha256. Signers MUST use rsa-sha256, and verifiers MUST be able to verify it.

rsa-sha1 MUST NOT be used for signing or verification. Signatures made with a historic algorithm, currently rsa-sha1, have permanently failed evaluation under RFC 6376.
sections.plainLanguage: Use rsa-sha256 to make DKIM signatures and make sure a verifier can check it. Do not use rsa-sha1 to sign or verify.

sections.title: RSA Key Sizes
sections.content:
Signers MUST use RSA keys of at least 1024 bits and SHOULD use keys of at least 2048 bits. Verifiers MUST validate keys from 1024 through 4096 bits and MAY validate larger keys.

Verifiers MUST NOT accept signatures made with RSA keys shorter than 1024 bits. The RFC describes key size as a trade-off among cost, performance and risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing keys must be at least 1024 bits, and keys of 2048 bits or more are recommended. A verifier must support keys from 1024 to 4096 bits and reject shorter ones.

sections.title: Security and Registry Update
sections.content:
This RFC does not change RFC 6376's security considerations. It reduces the risk of signature compromise from weak cryptography, and says the SHA-1 risks are addressed by no longer using rsa-sha1.

IANA updated the sha1 registration in the DKIM Hash Algorithms registry to show its status as historic.
sections.plainLanguage: The change removes rsa-sha1 from DKIM use to reduce risks from weak cryptography. IANA now labels the sha1 entry historic.
